summary:
MIDAS: Lunar Site Navigator is a website that displays the sunlight and Earth visibility for various locations on the Moon for different dates, using a year of hourly NASA/JPL Horizons data. The site is intended for use in exploring potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole, where the Sun and Earth stay low on the horizon and affect a lander’s solar power and contact with Earth.

The user can rotate the 3D model of the Moon, click on a location on the Moon, input coordinates manually, or select from 15 past landing sites. The user can also compare two sites or two dates.

The planning tools are Lunar Phases, Panoramic Sky View, Rise/Set Countdowns, and the Sunlight and Earth Visibility Charts for a 30-day window. The user can also change the assumed skyline angle to produce a simplified power and temperature estimate for a particular site.

MIDAS calculations are based on the assumption of a smooth sphere for the Moon; therefore, the terrain that is displayed does not cast shadows. Also, Earth visibility does not guarantee a radio link, and the calculated values for power and temperature do not represent the performance of any equipment. MIDAS is intended for planners, educators, and the general public to explore NASA data and trade-offs for lunar sites.
details:
What MIDAS does

MIDAS: Lunar Site Navigator allows users to explore the variation of sunlight and visibility of the Earth for various locations and times on the Moon. These variations are especially relevant for locations near the Moon’s south pole with low Sun angles and changing views of the Earth.

The user can rotate the 3D Moon and click to select sites or input coordinates of any site on the Moon. There are 15 past landing sites listed. The user can pin two sites for comparison. Also, the user can compare two different dates for the same site. The planning tools are a 30-day elevation chart, the lunar phases, a panoramic sky view, estimated rise/set countdowns, and cumulative sunlight and Earth-visibility durations.

How it works

The data used in MIDAS comes from NASA/JPL Horizons, which provides sub-solar and sub-Earth coordinates as well as the Earth–Moon distance for every hour for a full year from November 14, 2026, to November 14, 2027. Local spherical geometry uses this data to calculate the Sun’s and Earth’s elevations above the horizon and their compass bearings for a selected lunar site. Values between hourly samples are interpolated.

The Moon texture and landing-site coordinates are from NASA resources as well. The dates for lunar phases are from the U.S. Naval Observatory. These data are combined in the browser interface into interactive views that depend on the selected location and date.

Tools and development

The Lunar Site Navigator is written in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and uses Three.js for the interactive 3D view of the Moon. Python is used for downloading NASA data and preparing reference samples. All of the code is on GitHub, and the website is on GitHub Pages. The Lunar Site Navigator also includes automated tests that compare the results of the calculations with direct NASA/JPL Horizons surface-observer output, including the 15 catalog sites.

Creativity and intended impact

The tool provides a visual representation of the variation of sunlight and Earth visibility with respect to location on the Moon as well as time. It is intended for use by planners, educators, students, and the public to gain an understanding of the various factors that must be considered when selecting a site on the Moon.

Assumptions and limitations

Calculations are based on a smooth sphere. Terrain data is not used to calculate shadows. Local mountains, crater rims, slopes, and eclipses are not taken into account. Earth visibility is calculated on a geometric basis and does not guarantee a communication link. No allowance is made for relay satellites.

The tool can also vary the assumed skyline angle to produce simplified horizontal-panel power and reference-plate temperature estimates for stated assumptions. These estimates illustrate simplified assumptions and do not predict equipment performance. This is not intended to be a flight-planning tool. MIDAS is an educational exploration tool.

AI assistance and credits

Team MIDAS designed the project and reviewed the outputs. OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude were used for research, information gathering, coding assistance, debugging, troubleshooting, and checking the website and project demonstration. AI tools also assisted with presentation layout and illustrations.

Full data sources, software credits, and model assumptions are listed here:
https://github.com/pranavchilipiiiii/nasa_lunarmission/blob/main/SOURCES.md
